Time to Inactivity: Survival Analysis of US Grocery Loyalty Households

Kaplan-Meier, log-rank tests and Cox proportional hazards (R validation layer) on the Complete Journey data

Author

Household churn and lifetime value project

Published

October 15, 2026

Question, data and event definition

The Python models answer who is likely to be inactive in the 90 days after a cutoff. This report asks when households first go quiet and which early shopping behaviours are associated with that timing.

Data: the completejourney CC0 sample released by 84.51 (2,469 loyalty-card households, calendar year 2017, one retail chain). There is no subscription or cancellation record, so everything below is an inactivity proxy, not observed churn.

  • Event (lapse): the first gap between two shopping days longer than 90 days, starting at or after the landmark. A lapse is only confirmable if the 90-day gap fits inside the data, so households with no confirmable lapse are right-censored at data_end - 90 days.
  • Time origin: the first observed purchase. The panel starts on 2017-01-01, so this is not acquisition: households that already shopped before 2017 enter at their first 2017 purchase (left-censored tenure).
  • Landmark design: baseline covariates are measured over the 28 days after the origin and households enter the risk set at origin + 28 days. Covariates never use follow-up information, which avoids immortal-time bias.
  • Exclusions (counted, not hidden): households whose landmark falls after data_end - 90 (no time at risk) and households that already lapsed before the landmark.
  • Everything is an observational association. Nothing here is a causal effect of coupons or basket size.

Overall survival

2278 households analysed, 297 lapse events (13%), maximum follow-up 247 days after the landmark.

Code 
kable(rd("km_overall.csv"), digits = 3, caption = "Kaplan-Meier: share of households without a 90-day lapse")
Kaplan-Meier: share of households without a 90-day lapse
time survival lower upper n_risk
30 0.974 0.968 0.981 2210

90 0.934 0.924 0.944 2094
120 0.919 0.908 0.930 2043
180 0.889 0.876 0.902 1907

The curve is flat compared with a subscription business: most loyalty-card households keep shopping. The median time to lapse is not reached within the follow-up window, so we report survival at fixed horizons instead of a median.

Entry month group is partly a data-window artifact: households that first appear after January are lighter shoppers (median 2 baseline trips versus 4 for January entrants), as a household that shopped weekly would usually have appeared in January. It is therefore used as an adjustment variable, not interpreted as a cohort effect.

Proportional-hazards check (cox.zph)

Code 
kable(rd("cox_zph.csv"), digits = 4)
term chisq df p_value
log_trips 7.0209 1 0.0081
log_basket 0.4442 1 0.5051
fresh_10pts 0.4233 1 0.5153
coupon_user 0.0002 1 0.9893
store_pattern 1.0767 1 0.2994
entry_group 8.3566 2 0.0153
GLOBAL 18.9641 7 0.0083

The global test rejects proportional hazards (p < 0.01): baseline trip frequency (log_trips) and the entry group both show time-varying effects (see the Schoenfeld plots). The model is therefore refitted stratified on entry group, which brings the global test closer to non-significance, but the log_trips violation remains. Its hazard ratio should be read as an average effect over follow-up, not a constant one.

Sensitivity and limitations

Code 
cat(tail(readLines(file.path(out, "summary.txt")), 2), sep = "\n")
Sensitivity (Jan-2017 entrants only, n=1918, events=203): HR log_trips = 0.232 (main stratified: 0.253)
Demographics subset: n=798 households with income and age, events=8 (of 2278 analysed)
  • Lapse is a behavioural proxy; a household may return after 90 or more days (the event is “first lapse”, not permanent churn).
  • One calendar year only: follow-up is at most about 8 months after the landmark and tenure before 2017 is unknown.
  • Covariates are baseline-window only; the Python model uses time-varying behaviour.
  • Demographics cover 801 of 2,469 households and those households are heavier shoppers, with very few lapse events (see the line above), so no demographic survival model is fitted.
  • Results are associations, not causal effects of coupons, basket size or store pattern.
